question: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.

raiseTranscript.text: In my first internship, our test reports were manually copied from logs into a spreadsheet every day, which took hours. I wrote a 30-line Python script that parsed the logs and auto-generated the sheet.
What made it non-obvious?
The team assumed we needed a new tool or vendor; I realized the logs had consistent structure so regex plus pandas would work without any new dependencies.
What was the result?
Cut daily effort from 3 hours to 10 minutes. My manager had me teach the script to two other interns.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.
Intern automated daily log-to-spreadsheet reporting with a 30-line script
Quote: "Team assumed we needed a new tool; I realized regex plus pandas would work"
Follow-up: Asked what made it non-obvious → explained avoiding vendor dependency
Outcome: Reduced 3h to 10min; trained two other interns
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for junior. The story shows ownership of an individual task and a simple but non-obvious simplification that delivered measurable time savings. The candidate correctly identified that the team defaulted to buying a solution rather than looking at the data structure. Biggest strength is the willingness to ship a small, maintainable fix and then teach others.

lowerTranscript.text: We had slow page loads so I suggested we add caching, which the senior engineer implemented.
I just raised the idea in stand-up; they did the work.

junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for junior. The candidate did not own or create the solution; they merely named a standard technique already known to the team. No evidence of personal analysis or simplification work. The gap is lack of individual ownership and execution on the idea.

raiseTranscript.text: Two teams were duplicating customer profile data in separate services, causing sync bugs. Instead of adding another reconciliation job, I proposed we expose a lightweight shared view through an existing internal API and deprecate the duplicate stores.
How did you get buy-in?
I showed both teams the exact query patterns and the 4% error rate in a shared doc, then offered to own the migration for one service first.
Result?
Duplicate code removed from both services; incident rate dropped 60% over six months.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.
Proposed shared view via existing internal API instead of reconciliation job for duplicate customer data
Quote: "Showed both teams the exact query patterns and 4% error rate"
Follow-up: Asked how buy-in was secured → offered to own first migration
Outcome: Duplicate code removed; incidents down 60%
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for senior. The candidate identified a cross-team data duplication problem and chose a simplification path (reuse existing API) over the obvious new job. Evidence of influence without authority through data and willingness to take the first migration. Biggest strength is connecting the technical choice directly to a measurable reduction in incidents.

lowerTranscript.text: We had duplicate customer data so I built a nightly reconciliation job that synced the two services.
Why a new job instead of removing duplication?
That was the fastest way to stop the immediate incidents.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.
Built nightly reconciliation job for duplicate customer data
Quote: "That was the fastest way to stop the immediate incidents"
Follow-up: Asked why not remove duplication → chose speed over simplification
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for senior. The solution added operational complexity rather than removing the root duplication. No attempt to influence the owning teams or explore reuse of existing infrastructure. The gap is defaulting to the obvious incremental fix without considering simplification trade-offs.

raiseTranscript.text: My team was spending 30% of sprint capacity on manual QA for a legacy workflow. I asked them to spend one week mapping every manual step, then we replaced the workflow with a rules engine the support team could configure themselves.
How did you handle the team pushback?
Two engineers worried it would reduce their impact; I reframed the work as building a platform other teams would use and gave them ownership of the rules DSL.
Outcome?
Manual QA time dropped to under 5%; the rules engine is now used by three other teams.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.
Replaced manual QA workflow with configurable rules engine owned by support
Quote: "Reframed the work as building a platform other teams would use"
Follow-up: Asked how pushback was handled → gave engineers ownership of the DSL
Outcome: QA time to <5%; adopted by three other teams
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for manager. The leader created leverage by turning a team pain point into a reusable platform and addressed underperformance risk through role reframing. Clear team-level metric improvement plus cross-team adoption. Biggest strength is developing the team while delivering simplification at scale.

lowerTranscript.text: We had too much manual QA so I hired two more QA engineers to cover the load.
Headcount was the quickest way to protect velocity.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.
Hired two additional QA engineers for manual workload
Quote: "Headcount was the quickest way to protect velocity"
Follow-up: Asked about process change → no exploration of simplification
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for manager. The response solves the symptom with headcount instead of addressing the underlying manual process. No evidence of coaching the team toward higher-leverage work or creating team-level simplification. The gap is treating people as the only lever.

raiseTranscript.text: Customer support volume was growing 25% YoY while headcount budgets were flat. Instead of adding agents, we created a self-service diagnostic that used existing telemetry to auto-resolve 40% of tickets before they reached a human.
What made the approach non-obvious at the time?
Most leaders wanted more agents or an AI chatbot; we realized the telemetry already contained the signals needed for deterministic fixes.
Business impact?
Support cost per customer fell 18% while NPS held steady; the same pattern was later applied to two other workflows.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you came up with a creative or non-obvious solution to a problem.
Built self-service diagnostic from existing telemetry instead of adding agents or chatbot
Quote: "Telemetry already contained the signals needed for deterministic fixes"
Follow-up: Asked what made it non-obvious → rejected common AI/chatbot path
Outcome: Support cost per customer down 18%; pattern reused in two other workflows
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for exec. The leader rejected the obvious headcount or new-AI path in favor of a simplification that leveraged existing data, delivering clear cost leverage at business scale. Evidence of long-term thinking by designing a reusable pattern. Biggest strength is strategic judgment on where to apply creativity versus where to scale existing capability.

lowerTranscript.text: Support volume was rising so we launched a new AI chatbot that handled tier-1 questions.
Why a chatbot versus simplifying the product?
Chatbot was the fastest way to show progress on the cost problem.

exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for exec. The solution adds another system rather than reducing underlying complexity. No exploration of long-term leverage through product or process simplification. The gap is prioritizing visible activity over strategic trade-off analysis.
